findings.title: Backup code can be used without the account password
findings.body: Password verification is skipped whenever any totpCode is present (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`), while the new branch at line 131 accepts a backupCode independently of totpCode. A direct credentials request supplying a valid backupCode plus any non-empty dummy totpCode therefore skips verifyPassword entirely and logs in with the backup code as a single factor. Backup codes are long-lived recovery secrets meant to replace only the TOTP factor, not the password, so anyone who obtains one code (e.g. a photographed/stored list) gains full account access without knowing the password.

findings.title: Single-use backup code can be replayed by concurrent logins
findings.body: Consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write: authorize() reads user.backupCodes, checks indexOf, then updates the row nulling that entry. Two simultaneous login attempts with the same code can both read the pre-consumption value, both pass the check, and both write back an equivalent list, so the supposedly single-use code (promised as 'can be used exactly once' in the UI copy) authenticates more than once. Consumption needs an atomic/transactional compare-and-update or locking to guarantee one-time use.

findings.title: Backup-code comparison is case-sensitive and does not trim whitespace
findings.body: Codes are generated as lowercase hex and displayed/copyable as `XXXXX-XXXXX`, but verification only does `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` with no toLowerCase() or trim(). A user who transcribes the code in uppercase (as the placeholder's uppercase X styling suggests) or with surrounding whitespace is rejected with IncorrectBackupCode even though they typed the correct code, effectively locking recovery users out. The same un-normalized comparison exists in the disable endpoint (disable.ts line 61); normalize (trim + lowercase) in both places.

findings.title: Closing the modal on the backup-codes step desyncs 2FA state
findings.body: On successful enable the handler now only advances to DisplayBackupCodes and defers onEnable() (which refreshes the parent page's 2FA state) and resetState() to the explicit Close button (lines 261-270). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (X/Esc/backdrop via onOpenChange), the parent still shows 2FA as disabled even though the server enabled it, and the modal's step state remains DisplayBackupCodes, so reopening it lands on stale backup codes instead of the password step. onEnable/reset must also run on dialog close once enablement has succeeded.

findings.title: First 2FA test never dismisses the new backup-codes step and backup login is untested
findings.body: The 'enable 2FA and login using 2FA' test still proceeds straight from fillOtp to asserting the two-factor switch, but enabling now ends on the DisplayBackupCodes step and onEnable is only fired by the backup-codes Close button, so this test no longer drives the flow it asserts on. Only the second test was updated (download/copy/close), and the file itself notes at line 12 that login and disable with a backup code are untested. The new security-critical paths — successful backup-code login, rejection of a wrong code, and single-use invalidation of a consumed code — have no coverage, so regressions in them would ship undetected.
